object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer entity identified by account number. Every account is a distinct customer record, with account numbers never reused even if the same company returns.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number.
Six digits, sequential, never reused. If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an Account, six-digit sequential numeric code, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number.
Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: An agreement that an account pays a specified amount on a specified cycle for a product. Identified by a subscription ID prefixed with 'SUB'.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.
Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a Subscription, generated with SUB prefix.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offering. Currently three exist: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a Product.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that specifies what a customer pays and how often. Examples: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490. Each price plan points to exactly one feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
Every price plan gives you exactly one feature bundle.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a PricePlan.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a plan code

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: A feature bundle representing what a customer gets: the feature set including seats, API access, SSO. Examples: Starter, Professional, Enterprise. Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me.

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: The unique name identifying a FeatureBundle.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStartDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription begins. Always required.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: SubscriptionEndDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends. Optional; open-ended subscriptions have no end date.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The frequency of billing. Exactly one per subscription: monthly or annual only.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.
Only those two. There was a quarterly once, for one customer, and it caused so much trouble that we bought them out of it.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription. Exactly one: trialing, active, past due, or cancelled. Note: a separate boolean 'paused' flag exists but is not a status.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.
Exactly one, yes.
Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a plan change for a subscription. Captures the new price plan, effective date, and who requested it. Enables tracking of plan change history.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history.
It's got a change ID. It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a PlanChange.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date when a plan change takes effect, which may differ from the date it was requested.

source_references.excerpt: we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates. Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person or identifier of who requested a plan change.

The subscription is not merely a relationship but a business artifact with independent identity and lifecycle.

ambiguities.description: Three distinct concepts are all called 'plan' in common usage: (1) price plan (billing artefact with plan code), (2) feature bundle (what customer gets), and (3) sales deal (negotiated terms). The model uses 'PricePlan' and 'FeatureBundle' distinctly, but the domain does not have standard terminology to disambiguate. In implementation, developers may mistakenly conflate these concepts.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: The price plan... Tom: That's not what I mean by plan at all... When I say plan I mean what the customer gets... Priya: And I mean the billing artefact... Tom: And the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: Mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions has unclear commercial policy. The system rule is that cancellation sets an end date to the paid-through date and access continues with no automatic refund. However, four refunds were granted in the prior quarter as goodwill, contradicting the system behavior. Whether refunds are systematically allowed, case-by-case discretionary, or prohibited is undecided and must be resolved by finance and legal.

source_references.excerpt: Someone signs an annual deal in January, pays up front, cancels in April. What happens? Nothing happens... Tom: That's not what the pricing page implies... Tom: Four times in a quarter isn't goodwill, it's a policy nobody's written down... Facilitator: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: The 'paused' flag exists as a separate boolean attribute on subscriptions but overlaps semantically with status. A subscription with status 'active' and paused=true behaves like a paused status, but the system treats it as active. This dual representation causes bugs in querying. It is unclear whether 'paused' should be a fifth status value, remain a separate flag, or be eliminated.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: There's also paused. Priya: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The fact type 'Account holds Subscription' is objectified as the Subscription entity. However, the exact nature of objectification is implicit: Subscription is explicitly treated as an entity with its own ID and lifecycle, but the transcript does not clarify whether Subscription should have a separate reference_mode independent of Account, or whether it is solely identified by subscription_id. The model assumes subscription_id is globally unique, but this may need validation.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

ambiguities.description: The constraint 'one active subscription per account per product' is asserted as enforced at database level. However, the use of 'active' here is ambiguous: does it mean status='active', or does it mean 'not cancelled and not past-due'? The fact that a separate 'paused' flag exists and overlaps with 'active' status compounds this ambiguity. The model interprets 'active' as a logical concept that would need to be defined in the business rule, not strictly the status value.

source_references.excerpt: An account can have a subscription to each of them at once. So it's one active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level.

ambiguities.description: MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) is described as a derived field calculated from price plan and billing period, not stored. The calculation rule given (annual 490 → MRR 40.83) is clear, but the precise formula (e.g., annual / 12, with rounding rules) is not fully specified. If billing includes partial months, the derivation may be more complex than simple normalization.

source_references.excerpt: It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83... nothing writes it.

ambiguities.description: FeatureBundle is identified by name (Starter, Professional, Enterprise), but the transcript also mentions that 'there's no code, which annoys me' (product person). It is unclear whether future product development might assign bundle codes, and if so, whether the model should pre-emptively support an alternative or additional identifier.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me.

ambiguities.description: Account identification is stated as never reused. However, Tom notes (line 23) that from a product perspective, returning customers are the same entity, but reporting treats them as new due to the no-reuse rule. This creates a semantic gap: whether Account represents an operational customer record (with reusable IDs for tracking loyalty) or a financial account (with unique IDs per active business relationship) is not explicitly resolved. The model follows Priya's stated rule (no reuse), but this may create long-term data model friction.

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting... It drives finance the other way.

ambiguities.description: The 'plan_code' is stated as the reference_mode for PricePlan (e.g., CORE-MO-49). However, the transcript does not explicitly state that plan codes are globally unique or that they follow a strict format. The examples given follow a pattern (PRODUCT-PERIOD-PRICE), but whether all plan codes follow this pattern and whether the code itself is the identifier (vs. some other generated ID) is not fully clarified.
